albums.blurb: Mary Lattimore is a Los Angeles harpist who runs her concert harp through loop and effects pedals, building long-form pieces from layered phrases. Silver Ladders, her fourth studio album and released on Ghostly International, is the first she handed to an outside producer: Slowdive's Neil Halstead, who recorded it at his studio in Cornwall and added guitar and synthesizer, giving the record a mistier, shoegaze-tinted cast than her earlier self-recorded work. The album is entirely instrumental across its seven tracks.
albums.reception: Pitchfork rated Silver Ladders 7.7, praising Lattimore as an innovator who pushes past expectations of the instrument.

albums.blurb: The second album by Damon Albarn and Jamie Hewlett's animated band, and the moment the project outgrew its novelty framing. Largely produced by Danger Mouse, fresh off The Grey Album, it trades the debut's dub-pop sprawl for a darker, tighter song cycle threaded with guest turns from De La Soul, MF DOOM, Neneh Cherry, Roots Manuva, Ike Turner, Shaun Ryder, and Dennis Hopper. It remains the commercial and critical peak of the Gorillaz catalogue.
albums.reception: Lead single "Feel Good Inc." won the 2006 Grammy for Best Pop Collaboration with Vocals — the band's only Grammy to date — and the album went on to sell roughly eight million copies worldwide.

albums.blurb: Sade is the London band fronted by Nigerian-born singer Sade Adu, whose mid-80s hits like "Smooth Operator" defined sophisti-pop. Love Deluxe, their fourth album and first after a four-year silence, strips that sound to its most minimal: spacious bass, muted guitar, and Adu's cool, unhurried delivery on "No Ordinary Love," "Cherish the Day," and "Kiss of Life." It closed the band's classic run before an eight-year hiatus and became a touchstone for the neo-soul and quiet storm generations that followed.
albums.reception: Love Deluxe was certified quadruple platinum in the US, and "No Ordinary Love" won the 1994 Grammy for Best R&B Performance by a Duo or Group with Vocals.
